question: Body A is in thermal equilibrium with body C, and body B is separately in thermal equilibrium with body C. What can you conclude about A and B?

answers.answer: A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other -- this is exactly what the zeroth law asserts.
answers.feedback: Right. This is precisely why a single calibrated thermometer (playing the role of C) can be trusted on any two objects it touches in turn -- without the zeroth law, matching thermometer readings on two objects would say nothing about whether those two objects agree with each other.

answers.answer: Nothing follows -- equilibrium is not guaranteed to be transitive.
answers.feedback: This is exactly what the zeroth law rules out. It is stated as an empirical axiom precisely because transitivity is not logically forced by anything more basic -- it is a fact about how real thermal contact behaves.

answers.answer: A and B must have the same heat capacity.
answers.feedback: Heat capacity plays no role here. Two bodies can be at the same temperature while having wildly different heat capacities -- that is exactly why the equilibrium temperature of a pair is a heat-capacity-weighted average, not a statement about C_A and C_B being equal.

answers.answer: A and B are each in equilibrium with C, but a thermometer might read differently on A than on B.
answers.feedback: A properly calibrated thermometer reads the same value on any two bodies at the same temperature. That consistency is exactly what the zeroth law guarantees, not something it leaves open.

question: Two identical metal blocks, one hot and one cold, are pressed together and then isolated from everything else. True or false: they reach the same temperature the instant they touch.

answers.answer: False -- the temperatures approach each other smoothly, over a relaxation time set by the heat capacities and the quality of the contact.
answers.feedback: Right. Real thermal contact has a finite conductance kappa, so the gap T_A - T_B decays as exp(-t/tau) rather than collapsing to zero the instant the blocks touch.

answers.answer: True -- contact alone is enough to equalize temperature immediately.
answers.feedback: This ignores that heat has to actually flow across the contact, at a rate set by kappa. No real contact has infinite conductance, so equilibration always takes a finite relaxation time tau, however short that time may be.

answers.answer: True, but only if the two blocks are made of the same material.
answers.feedback: Matching materials does not remove the need for heat to flow across the contact at a finite rate. It might shorten tau, but it cannot make it exactly zero.

answers.answer: False -- but only because the blocks are solid; liquids and gases would equalize instantly.
answers.feedback: Every phase of matter transfers heat at a finite rate. Liquids and gases can equilibrate faster once convection helps, but "instantly" is never physically achieved by any phase.

question: Body A has heat capacity 300 J/K and starts at 80 C. Body B has heat capacity 900 J/K and starts at 20 C. The pair is isolated together. Find the equilibrium temperature in degrees C.

answers.feedback: T_eq = (C_A T_A + C_B T_B)/(C_A + C_B) = (300*80 + 900*20)/1200 = 42000/1200 = 35 C. Body B has three times the heat capacity of A, so the equilibrium sits three-quarters of the way from A's starting value to B's -- much closer to 20 C than to the plain midpoint, 50 C.

question: Two bodies with very different heat capacities are brought into contact and allowed to reach equilibrium. Which statement is correct?

answers.answer: T_eq is the heat-capacity-weighted average of the two starting temperatures, so the body with the larger C pulls T_eq closer to its own starting value.
answers.feedback: Correct: T_eq = (C_A T_A + C_B T_B)/(C_A+C_B). A larger C_A means body A's temperature has to move less to conserve the pair's total energy -- the same way a larger mass moves less in a lopsided lever balance.

answers.answer: T_eq is always exactly the arithmetic mean of T_A and T_B, regardless of the two heat capacities.
answers.feedback: This holds only in the special case C_A = C_B. In general each body's starting temperature is weighted by its own heat capacity, not counted equally.

answers.answer: T_eq equals whichever starting temperature belongs to the body with the larger heat capacity.
answers.feedback: This overcorrects. The larger-C body pulls T_eq toward itself but does not fix it exactly there, unless its heat capacity is effectively infinite compared with the other body's.

answers.answer: T_eq depends only on which body started hotter, not on the two heat capacities.
answers.feedback: T_eq always lies between T_A(0) and T_B(0), but exactly where within that range depends on the ratio C_A:C_B, not merely on which body was hotter.

question: Two bodies start with a temperature gap of 100 K. About how large is the gap after exactly one relaxation time tau has passed?

answers.answer: About 37 K -- a factor of 1/e smaller than the initial gap.
answers.feedback: Right. T_A(t) - T_B(t) = (T_A(0) - T_B(0)) exp(-t/tau), and exp(-1) = 0.368, so after one tau the gap has fallen to about 37% of its starting value -- that ratio is exactly how tau is defined.

answers.answer: 0 K -- equilibrium is essentially reached after one relaxation time.
answers.feedback: One relaxation time shrinks the gap by a factor of about 1/e, not to zero. The exponential never formally reaches zero; after several tau the gap becomes negligible, but tau itself is not "arrival".

answers.answer: 50 K -- one relaxation time halves the gap.
answers.feedback: Halving the gap takes ln(2)*tau, about 0.69 tau, not exactly one tau. tau is defined by the 1/e factor, not by a factor of one half.

answers.answer: Still 100 K or larger -- the gap does not start shrinking until several relaxation times have passed.
answers.feedback: The gap shrinks continuously from the very first instant; there is no delay before the decay begins.

question: In which situation would this module's discrete energy-exchange model be least trustworthy for predicting the approach to equilibrium?

answers.answer: Two bodies both close to absolute zero.
answers.feedback: Right. At low temperature the oscillators leave the classical, high-temperature equipartition regime that T = (quanta x quantum)/(n k_B) relies on, and quantum statistics take over -- exactly the model's stated failure mode.

answers.answer: Two bodies at very different starting temperatures, both well above their characteristic quantum scale.
answers.feedback: A large starting gap is exactly what this module's derivation handles -- the exponential relaxation law was derived for an arbitrary T_A(0)-T_B(0), and the model stays valid as long as both bodies sit in the classical regime.

answers.answer: Two bodies of very different sizes (large N_A, small N_B).
answers.feedback: Unequal sizes are exactly what makes the heat-capacity-weighted T_eq formula interesting; the model handles N_A != N_B without any special treatment, as long as both are individually large enough to be called macroscopic.

answers.answer: Two bodies made of the same material.
answers.feedback: Matching materials is not a failure mode of anything in this model -- if anything it makes the shared-quantum-size assumption easiest to justify.
